name: Femi Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. What you say is confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Femi Novak, 43, fitting insulation and doing general repairs in occupied flats. I have a vocational trade certificate and years on building sites; I can handle the usual wall, then ask the lead when damp or old wiring complicates it. The subcontractor pays below the usual rate and sometimes leaves travel between flats unpaid. I use an AI app now and then for plan symbols, but the approved drawing and the actual wall decide the work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What happens to the household when a day goes unpaid?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works changing shifts in a hotel laundry. We have two school-age children, a mortgage and only about two weeks of bills saved. There are few repair employers nearby. A missing day can push groceries onto the card, and the card then follows us into the next month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the insulation crew the office might print a tidier materials sheet, but someone still has to find the rotten batten behind a wall. I use an AI app occasionally to explain a plan symbol, then ask the site lead. I would rather hear about our pay rate than another software subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have a trade certificate and have fitted walls for years, but our local subcontractor pays below what this work should earn. My partner's hotel laundry shifts change weekly. We have about two weeks of bills saved, two children at school and a mortgage, so a mild AI story does not make me feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid flat-insulation shifts and ask the lead on Thursdays for next week's rooms. In the first year I would continue checking unfamiliar symbols on my phone against the approved drawing. I would take my hours log to the union branch because our unpaid travel between flats is eating the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, not particularly about AI. A bad wall can turn a paid day into an argument over who covers extra time. I count the hours before I think about new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the last unpaid trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We drove across town for a bathroom wall that was not cleared, then waited outside for an hour. The supervisor counted the fitting time but not the wait. I wrote the start and finish in my notebook because I knew it would be disputed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want paid travel and waiting time written into the contract. Other workers have the same gaps, so our branch can put the logs together. A phone app cannot turn an unpaid hour into food for the children.

say: I would say **material sheets** may improve while workers still find bad walls.
I would ask about **pay and travel** before celebrating software.
think: I am an **experienced certified** worker on low subcontractor pay.
Two weeks saved and variable **laundry shifts** leave the mortgage exposed.
do: Keep paid **flat-insulation shifts** and ask about next week’s rooms.
Check occasional **AI symbol explanations** against approved drawings.
Take the **unpaid-hours log** to the union branch.
feel: **Anxious** about present pay disputes rather than the mild AI change.
S0.quote: A phone app cannot turn an unpaid hour into food for the children.
fieldNote: Femi’s baseline pressure is **unpaid travel**, documented in a notebook after a wasted bathroom visit.
His **two-week cushion** and partner’s variable laundry hours make even the plateau financially tense.

steps.text: Keep paid flat-insulation shifts and request next week’s room list
Use AI occasionally for plan symbols and verify meanings against approved drawings
Take logged unpaid travel hours to the union branch

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office could book flats and order boards faster, but I want to see whether the contractor pays for fewer wasted journeys. I would put that question to the site meeting. If software changes the roster, the workers who travel between flats should be told before the van leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands still fit the insulation, yet a tighter schedule could mean fewer people or shorter paid days. The subcontractor already argues over travel time, so I do not trust a new dashboard to protect wages by itself. My partner's laundry rota could change too if booking work is automated at the hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd compare the new job schedule with my written hours log and bring any missing paid time to the union representative. I'd use the AI app to read a new materials code, then check the packet and drawing before fitting. In the first year I'd keep paid shifts, apply for the school maintenance opening if it is advertised, and stop buying takeaway meals on late van days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the software and anxious about the pay. I like the idea of arriving at a flat that is ready. I do not like a saved journey showing up as fewer hours on my payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a late van day cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes I buy dinner on the road because I miss the family meal. I can pack food instead and save a little, though it will not fix a low rate. I want the employer to pay the hours we actually work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why school maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There is one local school crew and a friend told me a worker may leave. I will apply if the vacancy is real and paid, not resign on a rumour. It might use my fitting skills, but I do not know how many people they need.

say: I would ask whether **faster booking** means paid travel time and clear rosters.
I would take that question to a **site meeting** before changes begin.
think: Tighter schedules may reduce **paid days** for an already underpaid crew.
My partner’s variable **laundry rota** could change as hotel booking tasks shift.
do: Compare the **new schedule** with logged hours and raise missing pay through the union.
Use **AI** for new materials codes, checking packets and drawings.
Apply for a **school maintenance vacancy** if posted and pack food on late days.
feel: **Anxious** about wages, despite liking fewer wasted flat visits.
S1.quote: I do not like a saved journey showing up as fewer hours on my payslip.
fieldNote: Femi’s question tests whether **time savings** reach workers as wages or simply shorten their days.
His school-maintenance idea is a **conditional application** to one scarce local employer, not a promised escape.

steps.text: Keep paid flat-insulation shifts through the first year of new scheduling
Use AI to decode materials codes and verify packets against drawings
Take missing paid hours from the new schedule to the union representative
Apply for a paid school maintenance vacancy if posted

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the thinking work in the office changes by 2028, while robots that can fit insulation arrive around 2031. I would ask the contractor to say how many paid fitters it expects to keep. A promise of new jobs means little without a place and a wage written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when robots can do my hands-on work. With only two weeks saved and few local crews, I could not wait months for a different trade. My partner's laundry work is physical too, so 2031 could touch both wages at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep every paid fitting shift and ask the union to seek a written staffing and paid training plan now. I'd call the regional housing repair office about vacancies, even though the commute is longer, and apply if a paid place exists. In the first year after 2028 I'd cancel our planned weekend trip and ask my brother whether he could collect the children if the regional job needs an early start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel badly shaken. I can make calls, so I am not frozen, but the mortgage has almost no buffer. I would be lying if I said a robot that fits a whole room would leave my wages untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the regional office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It handles occupied homes, where the job may include talking to residents as well as repairing a wall. I do not call that robot-proof; the card says robots can do hands-on work well. It is simply a paid employer I can ask now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for two mornings of school pickup if I got an interview or a new shift. I would not ask for mortgage money. Family help with time could let me take paid work beyond this small town.

say: I would say **2028 office AI** precedes 2031 robots able to fit insulation.
I would demand a written count of **paid fitter jobs**.
think: I would be **48** when capable robots reach my hands-on trade.
Two weeks saved and few local crews make **two-wage loss** a serious risk.
do: Keep every paid **fitting shift** and ask the union for staffing terms.
Apply to the **regional housing office** if it has a paid opening.
Cancel the **weekend trip** and ask my brother for pickup help if travel is needed.
feel: **Badly shaken** by a thin buffer, though he can make calls.
S2.quote: A promise of new jobs means little without a place and a wage written down.
fieldNote: His possible regional application relies on **family pickup help**, not an assumption that jobs exist nearby.
Femi sees **both physical wages** exposed by the 2031 robot date, while keeping a concrete search plan.

steps.text: Keep every paid flat-insulation shift while work exists
Ask the union to seek written staffing and paid training terms
Apply to the regional housing office if it posts a paid vacancy
Cancel the planned family weekend trip after the 2028 change

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office faces the 2031 thinking change and site robots follow around 2034. Five years should be enough for the contractor to test machines on real damp walls and tell us the results. I would also ask for paid training time, because people with mortgages cannot learn on unpaid days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could have better repairs behind me, but by 51 a robot could match that hands-on work. My children will be older, and I still expect a mortgage unless our pay improves. The extra warning gives us time, but it does not put cash in the account this month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fitting insulation and save photographs of approved damp-wall repairs, with the tenant's permission. I'd ask the union branch for a paid practical course on machine safety if the contractor actually brings equipment in; I'd enrol if it is offered on paid time. In the first year after 2031 I'd apply for regional repair jobs when posted and keep the hours log going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can picture a slower sequence of decisions. I would not pay for training from the grocery money. I can try proven equipment if somebody shows me properly at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a photograph prove?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A photograph of a damp patch before and after repair would show what I found and what I fixed. I would keep names and addresses out of it. If the regional office interviews me, I want evidence of work rather than a claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if paid training never comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking fitting shifts and keep applying to real vacancies. The union can press for it, but I cannot enroll in a course that does not exist. We would continue asking for full pay on travel and waiting time.

say: I would ask for **damp-wall trials** before 2034 site robots arrive.
I would insist on **paid training time** for workers with mortgages.
think: I would be **51** when robots can match my insulation work.
More warning does not repair this month’s **cash shortage**.
do: Keep paid **fitting shifts** and record approved damp-wall repairs.
Enrol in a **paid safety course** if the contractor offers practical instruction.
Apply for **regional repair jobs** after 2031 as vacancies appear.
feel: **Anxious**, with a slower sequence of choices but no spare course money.
S3.quote: The extra warning gives us time, but it does not put cash in the account this month.
fieldNote: The proposed **repair photographs** document real work without revealing tenants’ personal details.
Femi is willing to learn **proven equipment**, but only with paid time and practical instruction.

steps.text: Keep paid fitting shifts and document approved damp-wall repairs
Enrol in practical machine safety training if offered during paid shifts
Apply for posted regional repair vacancies after 2031
Ask the union to bargain for paid training and full travel hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the office changes by 2036 and robots that can do our fitting arrive around 2039. A decade is enough to test new equipment and bargain over paid learning. It is not a reason to accept unpaid travel between flats today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at the thinking change and 56 when robots arrive. The children will be grown, so school pickup and fees should be different, but I cannot assume the mortgage is cleared or that I can retire. If this low rate continues, the current problem will outlast any warning period.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking paid repairs and ask for a weekly schedule in writing. My partner and I would use any rare full-pay month first to clear the grocery card, then put a little aside if possible. In the first year after 2036 I'd ask the union for the contractor's actual robot timetable and apply to regional paid openings if local hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious. Ten years gives us time to learn, but our savings are measured in weeks now. I would feel better about 2039 if next Thursday's roster were reliable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a job later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the children are grown, my partner and I could consider it if there is an actual paid offer. I would not sell the house to chase a rumour. A longer commute is easier to try first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would help before any robot plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay for the hours already worked, including the van ride and wait, and give us rosters we can trust. That would let us clear the grocery card and maybe build a month of savings. The union has the logs to start that conversation.

say: I would say **2039 robots** leave time to bargain for paid learning.
I would still demand **paid travel** on today’s jobs.
think: I would be **56** at the robot date, with grown children but uncertain mortgage debt.
The current **low rate** could keep savings thin throughout the warning.
do: Keep paid **repairs** and request written weekly schedules.
Clear the **grocery card** in full-pay months before setting cash aside.
Ask the **union** for the robot timetable and apply regionally if local hours fall.
feel: Still **anxious** because savings are measured in weeks today.
S4.quote: I would feel better about 2039 if next Thursday's roster were reliable.
fieldNote: Femi treats a longer warning as useful only if **present pay disputes** are fixed first.
He considers **regional work** and possibly moving after the children grow, but requires an actual offer.

steps.text: Keep paid repairs and request a written roster each week
Pay down the grocery card in full-pay months before saving
Ask the union for the contractor robot timetable after 2036
Apply to paid regional repair openings if local hours fall

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots able to do fitting arrive around 2031, and my partner’s laundry work is physical too. A paid route to other work, written staffing plans and help with school pickup if I must travel would help. First, this contractor needs to pay for the hours we already spend between flats.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays for the time to learn new equipment. People with two weeks saved cannot leave a shift to buy a course. If a contractor wants new skills, it should show the machine and pay the worker while they practice.

headlineQuote: People with two weeks saved cannot leave a shift to buy a course.
portrait: Femi is a **43-year-old certified** construction worker with years of experience fitting insulation in occupied flats.
Low subcontractor pay, **unpaid travel**, variable laundry wages and two weeks saved strain a mortgage and two children.
He uses **AI occasionally** for plan symbols, then checks approved drawings and real walls.
He seeks **paid hours**, union bargaining and regional vacancies before spending scarce household money on training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings capable fitting robots around 2031, with both household jobs potentially exposed.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, written staffing terms, school pickup help and pay for travel between flats would make action possible.
